title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: without absolute elect-saving will grace no better prepared than in Adam
latin: Rat. 10. Si Christus non obtulerit seipsum Deo Patri cum peculiari quadam, & absoluta voluntate redimendi & efficaciter salvandi electos merito mortis suae; tum gratia efficax & vita aeterna non aliter praeparata esset, aut donata ullis hominibus in Christo, quam fuit in Adamo. Possibilitas enim habendi gratiam & vitam aeternam sub conditione ex libero arbitrio nostro pendente, in primo Adamo fuit concessa humano generi.
pass_a_gloss: Ratio 10. If Christ should not have offered himself to God the Father with a certain peculiar and absolute will of redeeming and efficaciously saving the elect by the merit of his death; then efficacious grace and eternal life would not otherwise have been prepared, or given to any human beings in Christ, than it was in Adam. For the possibility of having grace and eternal life under a condition hanging on our free choice was granted to the human race in the first Adam.
pass_b: Ratio 10. If Christ did not offer himself to the Father with a peculiar absolute will to redeem and save the elect efficaciously by his death's merit, then efficacious grace and eternal life would be prepared or given to no one in Christ on any better footing than they were in Adam. The first Adam already gave the race the chance of grace and eternal life under a condition that hangs on our free choice.

lemmas.form: non aliter … quam fuit in Adamo
lemmas.gloss: no otherwise than it was in Adam

notes_covered: Rat. 10 open; absolute elect-saving will; Adam parity premise

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: conditional-only merit leaves us no better off in Christ than in Adam
latin: Si ergo Christus morte sua non meruerit gratiam vitamque ullis hominibus absolute, sed omnibus promiscue sub hac incerta conditione, Si voluerint oblatam gratiam admittere, in ipsum credere, & in Fide perseverare, atque interim libero uniuscujusque arbitrio committat & relinquat, utrum velit credere, velit perseverare necne; profecto quod attinet ad ipsum modum & certitudinem obtinendae gratiae efficacis & vitae aeternae, nihilo meliore conditione uteremur in Christo, quam usi fuimus in Adamo.
pass_a_gloss: If therefore Christ by his death should not have merited grace and life for any human beings absolutely, but for all promiscuously under this uncertain condition—If they should have been willing to admit the offered grace, to believe in him, and to persevere in Faith—and meanwhile should commit and leave it to each one's free choice whether he wills to believe, wills to persevere or not; then indeed, as regards the very mode and certainty of obtaining efficacious grace and eternal life, we should use a condition no better in Christ than that which we used in Adam.
pass_b: So if by his death Christ did not merit grace and life for anyone absolutely, but only for all alike under the uncertain condition that they choose to receive the offered grace, believe in him, and persevere in faith, leaving to each person's free choice whether to believe and persevere, then we would be no better off in Christ than we were in Adam. That is so as to how and how surely we obtain efficacious grace and eternal life.

lemmas.gloss: we would enjoy a condition no better

notes_covered: conditional merit; free choice left decisive; no better condition in Christ

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: Adam parity contradicts Scripture’s sure purpose of good pleasure
latin: At hoc repugnat sacrae Scripturae, quae gratiam & vitam aeternam in Christo omnibus salvandis praeparatam & donandam suspendit ex certo proposito beneplaciti Divini, non ex contingente motu arbitrii humani; quod in controversia De Electione & Praeteritione ostendetur.
pass_a_gloss: But this conflicts with sacred Scripture, which suspends grace and eternal life prepared and to be given in Christ to all who are to be saved from the sure purpose of the Divine good pleasure, not from a contingent motion of human choice; which will be shown in the controversy Concerning Election and Passing-by.
pass_b: But that clashes with Scripture. Scripture hangs the grace and eternal life prepared and to be given in Christ to all who will be saved on God's sure purpose of good pleasure, not on a contingent turn of human choice. The treatise on Election and Passing-by will show this.

lemmas.gloss: from the sure purpose of the Divine good pleasure

lemmas.form: non ex contingente motu arbitrii humani
lemmas.gloss: not from a contingent motion of human choice

notes_covered: Scripture; purpose of good pleasure; Election & Praeteritione forward ref

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10: Augustine De corrept. & grat. 11—grace in Christ makes us will
latin: Repugnat etiam orthodoxorum Patrum sententiae, qui Pelagianis sese opposuerunt, ac nominatim Augustini, De corrept. & grat. cap. 11. ubi cum ostendisset, qualis ea gratia fuerit quae primo Adamo data fuit, De gratia praedestinatis in Christo praeparata & donata sic loquitur, Tanto amplius datur adjutorium gratiae per Jesum Christum, quibus id dare Deo placuit, ut non solum adsit sine quo permanere non possumus, etiamsi velimus, verum etiam tantum ac tale sit ut velimus. Est quippe in nobis per hanc Dei gratiam in bono recipiendo & perseveranter tenendo non solum posse quod volumus, verum etiam velle quod possumus.
pass_a_gloss: It also conflicts with the judgment of the orthodox Fathers who opposed the Pelagians, and namely of Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace chapter 11, where when he had shown of what sort that grace was which was given to the first Adam, concerning the grace prepared and given to the predestinate in Christ he speaks thus: So much more largely is the help of grace given through Jesus Christ to those to whom it pleased God to give it, that it not only is present without which we cannot remain, even if we should will, but also is so great and of such a kind that we will. For there is in us through this grace of God, in receiving the good and perseveringly holding it, not only to be able to do what we will, but also to will what we are able.
pass_b: It also clashes with the orthodox Fathers who opposed the Pelagians—above all Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace chapter 11. After showing what grace was given to the first Adam, he says of the grace prepared and given to the predestinate in Christ: “So much more largely is the help of grace given through Jesus Christ to those to whom God was pleased to give it, that it not only is present—without which we cannot remain even if we will—but also is so great and of such a kind that we will. For through this grace of God, in receiving the good and holding it perseveringly, there is in us not only the ability to do what we will, but also the will to do what we can.”

lemmas.gloss: so much more largely is the help of grace given
that we will … to will what we can

notes_covered: Fathers vs Pelagians; Augustine De corrept. & grat. 11; Adam vs Christ grace

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 10 close: elect-only fruitful application by special decree via Christ’s merit
latin: Haec gratia quae datur propter Christum solis electis, quaeque in illis solis producit effectum fructuosae applicationis & salutis, non ex speciali aliqua operatione arbitrii humani, sed ex speciali decreto voluntatis Divinae ad eos dimanat, idque mediante merito Christi. Ergo Christi meritum fuit iisdem speciali quodam modo a Deo destinatum, ab ipso Christo applicatum.
pass_a_gloss: This grace which is given on account of Christ to the elect alone, and which in them alone produces the effect of fruitful application and of salvation, flows to them not from some special operation of human choice, but from a special decree of the Divine will, and that by means of the merit of Christ. Therefore the merit of Christ was destined for the same persons in a certain special manner by God, applied by Christ himself.
pass_b: This grace, given for Christ's sake to the elect alone, and producing in them alone the fruitful application that saves, flows to them not from some special act of human choice but from a special decree of God's will, and that through Christ's merit. So Christ's merit was destined for those same persons in a special way by God, and applied by Christ himself.

lemmas.gloss: from a special decree of the Divine will

lemmas.form: speciali quodam modo a Deo destinatum
lemmas.gloss: destined by God in a certain special manner

notes_covered: elect-only grace; special decree; merit destined/applied; Rat. 10 close

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 11: equal divine efficacy left to human will is near-Pelagian
latin: Rat. 11. Est ea sententia a nobis rejicienda quae aut plane eadem est, aut saltem arctam habet cognationem cum damnato Pelagianorum dogmate: Illorum autem opinio, qui statuunt mortem Christi ex parte voluntatis & intentionis Divinae aequaliter se habere ad omnes quoad efficaciam, ex parte autem voluntatis humanae evenire, quod in eventu fiat efficax & fructuosa quibusdam, ad Pelagium quam proxime accedit. Orthodoxi autem, ad accuratam hujus rei considerationem a Pelagio expergefacti, & contra semper docuerunt, Fructuosam sive efficacem applicationem meritorum Christi a gratia praedestinationis pendere, per quam quibusdam misericorditer confertur Fides & ipsa bona voluntas, quae aliis justo Dei judicio denegatur.
pass_a_gloss: Ratio 11. That opinion is to be rejected by us which either is plainly the same as, or at least has a close kinship with, the condemned dogma of the Pelagians: but the opinion of those who state that the death of Christ on the side of the Divine will and intention stands equally toward all as to efficacy, yet on the side of the human will it comes about that in the event it becomes efficacious and fruitful for some, approaches Pelagius as nearly as possible. But the orthodox, awakened by Pelagius to an accurate consideration of this matter, have always taught against him that the fruitful or efficacious application of Christ’s merits depends on the grace of predestination, through which Faith and the good will itself are mercifully conferred on some, which by God’s just judgment is denied to others.
pass_b: Ratio 11. We must reject any view that is the same as—or at least close kin to—the condemned Pelagian dogma. Those who hold that on God’s will and intention Christ’s death stands equally efficacious toward all, while on the human will’s side it happens that in the event it becomes fruitful for some, come as near Pelagius as can be. The orthodox, roused by Pelagius to weigh this carefully, have always taught against him that fruitful application of Christ’s merits hangs on the grace of predestination, by which faith and even the good will itself are mercifully given to some and, by God’s just judgment, denied to others.

lemmas.form: arctam habet cognationem cum damnato Pelagianorum dogmate
lemmas.gloss: has close kinship with the condemned Pelagian dogma
depend on the grace of predestination

notes_covered: Rat. 11 open; near-Pelagian equal efficacy; predestination grace

title: Cap. 7 Rat. 11 close: Prosper/Hilary/Augustine/Fulgentius on special saving purpose
latin: Quod Pelagianum sit, fructum mortis Christi, id est, vitam aeternam, a speciali intentione Dei ad specialem operationem liberi arbitrii transferre, patet ex Prosperi Epistola ad Augustinum. Patet etiam ex Hilarii ad eundem Augustinum Epistola, ubi Reliquiae Pelagianorum in morte Christi vitam aeternam sic omnibus propositam & expositam opinantur, ut singulare aliquod sive speciale propositum Dei de salvandis electis per hanc mortem Christi prorsus pernegent, & totum hoc discrimen servatorum per mortem Christi & non-servatorum ad humanas voluntates revocent. Jam & contra, orthodoxos speciale & arcanum propositum agnovisse in Deo acceptante sacrificium mortis Christi, Christoque illud offerente, de applicatione ejusdem efficaci & fructuosa ad certas personas, non minus clarum est ex libris Augustini De Praedestinatione sanctorum, De Bono perseverantiae, aliisque contra Pelagianos & Semipelagianos conscriptis, in quibus haec, de speciali voluntate salvandi electos per Christum, si non unica, primaria tamen conclusio est. De Prospero & Fulgentio idem dici potest, qui passim asserunt efficacem salutis consecutionem in Christo ab efficaci & speciali voluntate Divina Christum electis speciali modo destinante, non a libero hominum arbitrio Christi mortem ac merita sibi, prout contigerit, applicante.
pass_a_gloss: That it is Pelagian to transfer the fruit of Christ’s death, that is, eternal life, from the special intention of God to a special operation of free choice, is plain from Prosper’s Letter to Augustine. It is plain also from Hilary’s Letter to the same Augustine, where the Remnants of the Pelagians think eternal life so proposed and set forth to all in Christ’s death that they utterly deny any singular or special purpose of God concerning saving the elect through this death of Christ, and recall this whole discrimination of those saved through Christ’s death and of the unsaved to human wills. And on the contrary, that the orthodox recognized a special and hidden purpose in God accepting the sacrifice of Christ’s death, and in Christ offering it, concerning its efficacious and fruitful application to certain persons, is no less clear from Augustine’s books On the Predestination of the Saints, On the Good of Perseverance, and others written against the Pelagians and Semipelagians, in which this—concerning the special will of saving the elect through Christ—if not the only, is nevertheless the primary conclusion. The same can be said of Prosper and Fulgentius, who everywhere assert that the efficacious obtaining of salvation in Christ is from the efficacious and special Divine will destinating Christ to the elect in a special manner, not from human free choice applying Christ’s death and merits to themselves as it may chance.
pass_b: That it is Pelagian to shift the fruit of Christ’s death—eternal life—from God’s special intention to a special act of free choice is plain from Prosper’s Letter to Augustine. Hilary’s Letter to Augustine shows the same: the Pelagian remnants treat eternal life in Christ’s death as so set before all that they flatly deny any singular purpose of God to save the elect by that death, and put the whole divide between the saved and the unsaved down to human wills. Against them, the orthodox saw a special hidden purpose in God accepting Christ’s death-sacrifice and in Christ offering it—toward efficacious fruitful application to certain persons. That is clear from Augustine’s On the Predestination of the Saints, On the Good of Perseverance, and his other anti-Pelagian and anti-Semipelagian books, where the special will to save the elect through Christ is if not the only then the chief conclusion. Prosper and Fulgentius say the same throughout: efficacious obtaining of salvation in Christ comes from God’s efficacious special will destinating Christ to the elect in a special way, not from human free choice applying Christ’s death and merits to itself as chance may have it.

lemmas.form: ad specialem operationem liberi arbitrii transferre
lemmas.gloss: to transfer to a special operation of free choice

lemmas.form: non a libero hominum arbitrio … applicante
lemmas.gloss: not from human free choice applying

notes_covered: Prosper; Hilary Reliquiae; Augustine Pred./Persev.; Fulgentius; before ultimum Patrum
